title: Fewest Single-Letter Gene Edits
statement:
A gene is a string of exactly 8 letters, each one of A, C, G, T. One edit changes a single letter of a gene into another of those four letters.

You get a start gene, an end gene and a list bank of allowed genes. Every gene produced by an edit, including end itself, must be in bank. The start gene does not need to be.

Return the smallest number of edits that turns start into end, or -1 if it cannot be done. If start equals end, the answer is 0.

examples.why: Change the 5th letter then the last (via ACGTTCGT), or the other way round (via ACGTACGA).
Only 2 letters differ, but neither direct middle step is allowed. The detour AAAAAAAG → AAAAAACG → AAAAAACC takes 3 edits.
The end is allowed, but one edit cannot reach it and no gene in between is in the bank.

constraints: All genes use only A, C, G and T
hints: Think of every gene as a node, with an edge between genes one edit apart. What are you looking for in that graph?
The fewest edits is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, so breadth-first search fits.
Put the bank in a set. From a gene, generate the 8 × 3 = 24 one-letter variants and keep those in the set that you have not visited.

explain.intuition:
Each allowed gene is a node, and two genes are connected when they differ in exactly one letter. Every edge costs one edit, so the fewest edits is the shortest path from start to end, and breadth-first search finds it level by level.

Finding neighbours by comparing against the whole bank costs O(bank) per node. Generating them instead is cheaper: a gene has only 8 positions × 3 other letters = 24 possible neighbours, and a set tells you in O(1) whether each one is allowed. It is the same move as building a lookup map instead of scanning a list on every render.
steps: If start == end, return 0. Put the bank in a set; if end is not in it, return -1.
BFS from start with a queue of genes and a step counter, and a visited set.
For each gene in the current level, try all 24 single-letter changes. A change equal to end returns steps + 1. Other changes that are in the bank and not yet visited join the next level.
pitfalls: Returning the number of differing letters. The second example needs a detour, so the answer can be larger.
Requiring start to be in the bank. It is only the starting point.
Marking genes visited when you pop them instead of when you push them, which can add the same gene many times.

complexity.time: O(B · 8 · 4) for a bank of B genes

solutions.title: BFS comparing with the whole bank
solutions.idea: BFS where the neighbours of a gene are found by checking every bank gene for exactly one differing letter.

solutions.title: BFS generating neighbours
solutions.idea: From each gene, try all 24 single-letter edits and keep those in the bank set.

followups: Search from both ends at once. Why does bidirectional BFS help when the branching factor is large?
Some edits cost more than others (say, A↔G is cheaper). Which algorithm replaces BFS?
